extracted.intended_audience: parties and practitioners in inter partes review proceedings (petitioner, patent owner, patent attorneys), and PTAB judges/staff
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and legal criteria used by the Patent Trial and Appeal Board to evaluate patent claim patentability (anticipation and obviousness), including claim construction, burdens of proof, and supporting evidentiary and procedural rules, as applied in an inter partes review remand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction standard for pre-November 13, 2018 IPRs
rubrics_metrics.description: In an inter partes review proceeding based on a petition filed prior to November 13, 2018, the Board interprets claims of an unexpired patent using the broadest reasonable construction in light of the specification in which they appear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 37 C.F.R. § 42.100(b) (2017); Cuozzo Speed Techs., LLC v. Lee, 136 S. Ct. 2131, 2144–46 (2016) (upholding the use of the broadest reasonable interpretation standard). A subsequent amendment to the regulation does not apply to petitions filed before November 13, 2018.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary and customary meaning when no construction necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: If a party asserts that 'no constructions are necessary,' claim terms take on their ordinary and customary meaning that the terms would have to one of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties may propose that claim terms be given ordinary meaning; the Board will construe terms where necessary (see example where 'rate' was construed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation under 35 U.S.C. § 102
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is unpatentable as anticipated under 35 U.S.C. § 102 if a single prior-art reference expressly or inherently describes each limitation set forth in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Perricone v. Medicis Pharm. Corp., 432 F.3d 1368, 1375 (Fed. Cir. 2005); Verdegaal Bros., Inc. v. Union Oil Co. of Cal., 814 F.2d 628, 631 (Fed. Cir. 1987). The Board will compare the claim limitations to the prior-art reference(s) and determine whether each limitation is described. Part-time satisfaction (e.g., a prior-art system that sometimes practices the claimed limitation) can be sufficient to establish anticipation (Hewlett-Packard Co. v. Mustek Sys. Inc., 340 F.3d 1314).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness under 35 U.S.C. § 103 (Graham framework)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is unpatentable for obviousness under 35 U.S.C. § 103 if the differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Graham factors: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between claimed subject matter and prior art; (3) level of skill in the art; (4) objective evidence (secondary considerations). See KSR Int’l Co. v. Teleflex Inc., 550 U.S. 398, 406 (2007). The obviousness inquiry typically requires an analysis of whether there was an apparent reason to combine known elements in the fashion claimed; courts require 'articulated reasoning with some rational underpinning' (In re Kahn, 441 F.3d 977, 988).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to articulate reason to combine references
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevail on obviousness, a petitioner must show why a person of ordinary skill would have been motivated to combine prior art references in the particular manner claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR requires an analysis of 'whether there was an apparent reason to combine the known elements in the fashion claimed by the patent at issue.' Mere conclusory statements are insufficient (In re Magnum Oil Tools Int’l, Ltd., 829 F.3d 1364, 1380). The Board looks for articulated reasoning with a rational underpinning (In re Kahn).

rubrics_metrics.name: Petitioner's burden of proof and particularity requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: In an inter partes review, the petitioner must demonstrate by a preponderance of the evidence that the challenged claims are unpatentable, and the petitioner has the burden from the onset to show with particularity why the patent is unpatentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 35 U.S.C. § 316(e); 37 C.F.R. § 42.1(d). Petitions must identify 'with particularity... the evidence that supports the grounds for the challenge to each claim' (Harmonic Inc. v. Avid Tech., Inc., 815 F.3d 1356, 1363). The burden never shifts to Patent Owner (Dynamic Drinkware, LLC v. Nat’l Graphics, Inc., 800 F.3d 1375).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on relying on conclusory statements
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner does not satisfy its burden of proving obviousness by employing mere conclusory statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Magnum Oil Tools Int’l, Ltd., 829 F.3d 1364, 1380 (Fed. Cir. 2016). The Board requires factual and logical support for combinations and conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of ordinary skill in the art as an evidentiary factor
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board adopts a factual finding describing the level of ordinary skill in the art (education/experience) as part of the obviousness analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical formulation: e.g., 'a B.S. degree in computer science or electrical engineering (or comparable degree) and two years of experience in networking or streaming media, or an M.S. in computer science or electrical engineering (or comparable degree).' Such characterizations are approximate and may be adjusted by showing higher education can make up for less experience and vice-versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Part-time practice in prior art can establish anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art that only sometimes embodies a claimed method or limitation can nonetheless teach that aspect of the invention and establish anticipation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authority: Hewlett-Packard Co. v. Mustek Sys. Inc., 340 F.3d 1314 (Fed. Cir. 2003). The Board analogously applies this principle to software aspects of apparatus claims: the mere fact that a prior-art server might sometimes transmit slower does not negate that it also contains instructions to transmit faster when it does so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible supplementation of arguments on reply and remand
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments and responsive evidence raised in a reply (or on remand) may be considered by the Board; the institution decision need not anticipate every legal or factual issue that might arise in the course of trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities: Idemitsu Kosan Co., Ltd. v. SFC Co. Ltd., 870 F.3d 1376, 1381; Genzyme Therapeutic Prod. Ltd. P’ship v. Biomarin Pharm. Inc., 825 F.3d 1360, 1366. The Board may permit simultaneous remand briefing addressing issues identified by an appellate court's claim construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid importing additional limitations beyond court construction
rubrics_metrics.description: In construing claim terms and assessing prior art disclosures, one must not improperly import additional limitations into the claim beyond the court's construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Patent Owner attempted to read a requirement that 'each' requested media data element must be sent faster than playback into the Federal Circuit's construction of 'rate'; the Board rejected importing that additional requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of secondary references to supply well-known options
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a prior art reference does not expressly disclose a limitation, a petitioner may rely on other well-known sources (e.g., standards) to supply that limitation if there is a motivation to do so and it would have been obvious to a POSITA to combine them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: using ISO-11172 as a source to modify Carmel to use a constant bit rate as 'one of the well-known options' of MPEG and 'for the purposes of supporting a wider variety of [media data].' The Board concluded this provides motivation under §103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board will consider dependent-claim limitations by reference
rubrics_metrics.description: For dependent claims, the Board may rely on analysis provided for corresponding limitations in other claims and petition references; lack of a separate response from Patent Owner on dependent claims does not preclude the Board from finding them unpatentable if the petitioned analysis supports that conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision reviewed dependent-claim mappings to earlier-analyzed claim limitations and found Carmel disclosed respective limitations when the petition provided the cross-reference analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies and post-decision procedural notices
rubrics_metrics.description: If Patent Owner wishes to pursue amendment of challenged claims outside the IPR (e.g., reissue or reexamination) after issuance of a final written decision, specific Notices and obligations apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See April 2019 Notice Regarding Options for Amendments by Patent Owner Through Reissue or Reexamination During a Pending AIA Trial Proceeding (84 Fed. Reg. 16,654 (Apr. 22, 2019)). If filing a reissue application or request for reexamination of the challenged patent, Patent Owner must notify the Board of related matters in updated mandatory notices (37 C.F.R. § 42.8(a)(3), (b)(2)).
